transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-02-14
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Ben Carter (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Rajat Sharma (Head of ML - Elysian), Emily Park (Platform Eng - Elysian), Liam O'Neil (CTO - Elysian)

Summary:
Short discovery focused on integration patterns for Redwood hosted vs dedicated vs private for a vector search / RAG workload. Key topics: SDKs, LangChain/LlamaIndex connectors, gateway/proxy architecture, rate limits/quotas, observability/tracing hooks, VPC/KMS for private deployments. Next steps agreed (pricing, integration repo, bench).

Transcript:
[00:00] Ben: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Ben Carter from Redwood, AE on this account, and with me is Maya Singh, our systems SE. How's everyone?
[00:10] Rajat: Hi Ben, hi Maya. Rajat here. Thanks for running through this. We wanted to focus on how we'd integrate Redwood into our existing RAG stack.
[00:20] Ben: Great. Could you give a quick overview of your current infra and what you're trying to solve?
[00:27] Rajat: Sure. We're Elysian Networks, we run a couple of services that do network telemetry analysis. We have a vector DB (Pinecone for now) with about, uh, 12M vectors, using OpenAI embeddings for now but exploring running embeddings in-house. Our app does real-time retrieval-augmented generation for customer support and automated triage, so latency and throughput matter.
[00:45] Emily: On infra side, we use AWS, VPCs, SSO via Okta, and KMS for encryption. We're sensitive about data custody — some of our customers require no data leaving our VPC.
[00:58] Maya: Cool, thanks. So main themes I hear: 1) RAG pipeline with vector store, 2) embeddings and LLM inference, 3) strict networking and KMS needs. Does that sound right?
[01:06] Liam: Yep. Also looking at cost — we plan to scale to ~200 qps peak across microservices and want predictable billing.
[01:15] Ben: Perfect. A couple of quick product notes: Redwood has three deployment modes — Hosted API (fastest), Dedicated (reserved GPU pools for predictable throughput), and Private (VPC/on-prem for full network isolation + KMS integrations). For a setup like yours with strict VPC/KMS needs, Private is commonly used but Dedicated with VPC peering can also work depending on data residency.
[01:36] Rajat: Can you clarify the difference wrt integration? Like, if we use Redwood hosted, we call your public API via SDK. For Dedicated/Private, is the SDK the same?
[01:45] Maya: Good q. The SDK surface is consistent across modes — same REST/SDK calls for generation, chat, embeddings. The difference is in auth + network path: hosted uses API keys and public endpoints; Dedicated gives you a dedicated model endpoint with reserved throughput and role-based API keys; Private has a customer-controlled control plane and options for VPC endpoints, private link, or on-prem gateways. So your developer integration code stays mostly identical, which helps.
[02:10] Ben: We also support first-class wrappers for LangChain and LlamaIndex — there's a maintained Redwood LLM wrapper that you can drop into LangChain chains or LlamaIndex nodes. Maya can share the example repo.
[02:22] Emily: Awesome. Are those wrappers streaming-safe? We do streaming to reduce perceived latency in our UI.
[02:28] Maya: Yes — streaming is supported across hosted/dedicated/private. For LangChain, the async callback handlers work; for LlamaIndex, we have example generators that stream tokens back and you can wire them into your SSE endpoint. Sometimes the transcripts out of the auto transcribe have small artifacts, but the token stream is consistent.
[02:45] Rajat: About embeddings: do you recommend using Redwood embeddings or bringing our own? We may want to run embeddings in-house for cost reasons.
[02:53] Ben: You can do either. Redwood offers an embeddings endpoint and we publish the model dims and perf. If you want to run embeddings in your VPC, the Private option or Dedicated with private link is common. Also if you run your own embedding model, you can still use Redwood for generation and the SDK supports multiple endpoints.
[03:10] Liam: We rely on LangChain + LlamaIndex glue code today. Any gotchas integrating stateful stores like our Pinecone and the Redwood SDK?
[03:18] Maya: Not many. Typical pattern is: use your vector DB for retrieval, then call Redwood generation with the top-K contexts. For LlamaIndex, you can plug Redwood as the LLM predictor. One thing to note: prefix/KV cache behaviors when you use streaming + long contexts — Redwood's runtime optimizes KV cache usage but you want to pass consistent metadata to maximize cache hits. E.g., stable prompt templates, same system messages.
[03:42] Rajat: Metadata — do you pass X-Request-ID or trace headers so we can correlate across services?
[03:47] Maya: Yep. We support standard tracing headers (traceparent, x-request-id) and you can pass customer metadata headers that show up in logs in the Console. We also emit per-request token counts and cost estimates in the audit logs.
[03:58] Emily: On quotas/rate limits: we need per-team and per-route quotas. Can Redwood do per-API-key quotas to limit spend and protect model access?
[04:06] Ben: Yes, our rate-limiting supports per-key quotas, per-route limits, and burst configs. For Dedicated customers we can size GPU pools to meet sustained throughput; the quota enforcement sits above that so you can throttle different teams differently.
[04:18] Rajat: What's the latency profile? We're targeting p50 < 200ms for short prompts and p95 < 800ms for standard RAG snippets.
[04:28] Maya: Depends on model + sequence length + batching. For small context calls on a smaller model we can easily hit ~100-200ms p50 in Dedicated; hosted latencies vary with multi-tenant load but we publish performance profiles. We'll propose a benchmark run where you send sample prompts.
[04:45] Liam: About gateway/proxy patterns: our infra team prefers a sidecar or gateway to centralize auth and rate-limiting. Any recommendations?
[04:53] Ben: Many customers use a gateway/proxy in front of Redwood to implement auth, consistent headers, and additional logging. The tradeoff is you add one extra network hop and complexity. Alternatively, you can use our client-side SDK plus API key rotation and per-key quotas. If you want to centralize observability, a proxy makes sense; if you want minimal hop and simpler tracing, direct SDK calls are simpler.
[05:15] Emily: We also need audit logs with export to our Splunk/Datadog. Is that supported?
[05:20] Maya: Yes — Console has logs and you can stream audit logs to our S3 export or push to your SIEM via webhooks. You can get token-level cost breakdown, user keys, request metadata. We also support exporting traces (OpenTelemetry).
[05:33] Rajat: Security: SOC2, HIPAA, and KMS integrations — do you have SOC2 attestation and support customer-managed keys?
[05:40] Ben: Redwood is SOC2 Type II certified. For customer-managed keys, Dedicated and Private support KMS/HSM integrations — you can bring your own keys in Private deployments. We'll share the security pack with the SOC2 report redacted.
[05:53] Liam: If we do a Private deployment, how are upgrades/patches handled? We want predictable maintenance windows.
[06:00] Maya: For the Private control plane we have contracts that specify maintenance windows; upgrades are scheduled with you and we support canary rollouts. There is also an on-prem package if you need air-gapped.
[06:10] Rajat: A practical question: our devs use LangChain async chains heavily and LlamaIndex for docstore orchestration. Are there pre-built examples for both?
[06:18] Maya: Yes — we have two example repos: one for LangChain async chains and streaming callbacks, the other for LlamaIndex integration with node-based indexing and retrieval. They demonstrate the Redwood LLM wrapper, embedding flows, and a small benchmark harness. I'll share links.
[06:31] Rajat: Good. Can we run an initial bench at low cost? Ideally you spin up a dedicated trial or we run against hosted with some rate limits.
[06:38] Ben: We can offer a short dedicated trial for a week or run a hosted benchmark with constrained throughput. For more realistic p95 numbers I'd recommend a small dedicated pool. We'll include trial options in the pricing sheet.
[06:50] Emily: How do you handle model fallbacks? Say primary model is out of capacity, do you have automatic fallbacks to cheaper models?
[06:57] Maya: Yes — smart routing can fallback by policy to compatible model variants or to a different region. You can configure automatic fallback tiers per route.
[07:06] Rajat: Any notes about tokenization differences? We're sensitive about token counting mismatch between embedding models and generation models.
[07:12] Ben: We publish tokenizers and token-counting utilities in the SDK to normalize counts across models. Also our Console reports token usage per request.
[07:20] Liam: For instrumentation we want per-request traces, sampling, and alerting for error rates and latency. Are there SLO/alert hooks?
[07:28] Maya: You can define alerts around latency and error thresholds. We can push metrics to Datadog, or you can use webhook alerts. The Console also has route-level dashboards showing tokens, p50/p95 latency, and error breakdown.
[07:40] Rajat: There may be procurement constraints — we need PO support and a standard MSLA for Dedicated.
[07:46] Ben: We have an enterprise contract addendum and procurement playbook; we can share sample MSLA and PO terms.
[07:53] Emily: A nit: rate-limits in hosted mode — what happens when we hit the quota? 429 or queued?
[07:58] Maya: Hosted returns 429s; we can also offer token-bucket bursts and queueing for Dedicated if you want a soft buffer.
[08:06] Rajat: Ok that helps. On the LLM side, do you support function calls / structured outputs for our orchestration layer?
[08:14] Maya: Yes, function/tool calling is supported. We also have structured output helpers in the SDK to validate schema and parse outputs safely.
[08:22] Ben: Let's recap and outline the next steps. We'll send pricing and sizing options, Maya will share LangChain/LlamaIndex example repos and webhook + tracing docs. We'll schedule a deep-dive benchmark once you share sample payloads and allowed test window.
[08:36] Rajat: Sounds good. Couple quick clarifications before close— for Dedicated trials what's the lead time?
[08:42] Ben: For small dedicated pools we can spin up in days; larger reserved capacity has a longer lead time (weeks) depending on region and GPU availability.
[08:50] Liam: And SLAs for Dedicated?
[08:53] Ben: SLA depends on commitment level; standard Dedicated SLA includes uptime and latency targets — details will be in the pricing doc.
[08:59] Emily: Network-wise we'll check if VPC peering or PrivateLink is preferred — we'll confirm with infra and get back.
[09:05] Ben: Great — appreciate the time. We'll follow up with the docs and repo links.
[09:10] Rajat: Thanks Ben, Maya.
[09:12] Ben: Thanks everyone, talk soon.

Post-call notes:
- Customer interested in Private or Dedicated (due to KMS/VPC) but open to hosted for initial bench.
- Integration path: LangChain and LlamaIndex wrappers will simplify adoption — share repos.
- Observability needs covered via trace headers, OpenTelemetry, logs export, and alerting webhooks.
- Bench next steps: Elysian to provide sample prompts and QPS targets; Redwood to propose trial configuration and pricing.
